text:
A: Hello, my love! Can you hear me alright? I'm Debbie.
B: Hello. Yes, I can hear you. I'm Hira.
A: Oh, that's a lovely name. Sorry, I'm still sat in the kitchen, so you'll have to excuse the mess behind me. The craft box has been out since Tuesday.
B: No, it's fine. I saw it in your photo, I think. Is it for cards?
A: That is, yes! Card-making. Well, I say card-making. I've got a whole drawer full of kits I've started and not finished, do you know what I mean? I get to the glitter bit and lose interest.
B: I have the same with crochet. I have a blanket that has taken three months.
A: Three months! But at least you're still going with it. What colours?
B: Grey and mustard. It's for, erm, just for our sofa, I think. Usually I make small things for colleagues when they have babies. Hats, little blankets.
A: Oh, that's ever so kind. They must love that. Where do you work, then, love?
B: At the hospital in Reading. In the pharmacy, on the wards.
A: I said you looked clever, with all them big books behind you. I did, I put that on the form.
B: They are mostly heavy, not clever.
A: Do you do the old people's wards and that?
B: Yes, quite a lot of the medical wards. Many older patients. Later I'd like to specialise in care of the elderly, maybe.
A: Ah. My mum was in and out of hospital at the end. She had dementia. That's five years ago now. The nurses were lovely with her, they really were. I don't know how you all do it, honestly.
B: I'm sorry about your mum. Dementia is very hard. For the families especially.
A: That is. Anyway, sorry, love, I'm going all gloomy on you. Where are you from originally, if you don't mind me asking?
B: Pakistan. Faisalabad. I came here seven years ago.
A: Seven years! And do you get back much?
B: Once a year, normally, for two or three weeks. My parents are there, and one sister. I talk to my sisters on video at the weekends. Sometimes my sister sends voice notes at three in the morning, our time.
A: Oh, that's the time difference, isn't it! My sister's only round the corner, so she just turns up. I've got nearly all my family within a few miles, you know. I'd be lost without them. Do you miss your mum?
B: Yes. More than I say, I think. Mostly I miss her cooking. I'm still trying to make my chapatis as round as hers.
A: Oh, bless you. Mine would come out the shape of Norfolk. What do you cook, then?
B: Daal, aloo gosht, mostly Punjabi food. And on Sundays a roast chicken, because my mother-in-law likes it.
A: Ooh, a roast! Do you do Yorkshires?
B: Erm, I tried once. They didn't rise. Na, they were flat.
A: That's the oven, love. You want it ever so hot, and the oil smoking before the batter goes in. That's the secret, that is. My Steve won't have a Sunday without them.
B: Okay. Very hot. I'll try that. Thank you.
A: And don't open the door! That's where everybody goes wrong, they peek.
B: I think I peeked.
A: Everybody does, love. Do you walk at all? I take Tilly, my dog, along the seafront every day. She's got a bad hip, but she still drags me out.
B: Yes, I walk by the river on the Thames Path, or round the lake near us. It's nice when it's not raining, which is not often.
